BIOLOGICAL WARFARE EXPERIMENTS
speechtext:
1.	Have any biological warfare experiments or research been carried out in Canada in 1956 or 1957, under the direction of American (U.S.A.) scientists?
2.	If so, under what agreement or agreements were these arrangements made?
3.	How many American scientists have been involved in such experiments?

speakeroldname: Hon. G. R. Pearkes (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: BIOLOGICAL WARFARE EXPERIMENTS
speechtext:
The answer to the first part of the question is no. The second and third parts of the question are not applicable in view of the answer to the first part of the question. However, in fairness to the hon. member who asked the question I should say that during this period United States scientists have assisted in biological warfare experiments, but the work was at all times and at all stages under the direction of Canadian scientists. This assistance was provided under the basic standardization agreement among the armies of the United States, United Kingdom and Canada, 1954. Seven American scientists assisted in these experiments for a period of about four months during the winter of 1956-57.

With reference to section 60 of the Auditor General's Report, 1957:
1.	What official of the Department of National Defence authorized the expenditure of some $2,068,000 for the joint maritime warfare school at Halifax?
2.	To whom was the original contract of $750,000 awarded?
3.	Was this project abandoned?
4.	If so, on what date, and what was the total expenditure on the project up to time of abandonment?
5.	What was the cost of the building erected to house this project?
6.	What use is being made of the building?

speakeroldname: Hon. G. R. Pearkes (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the answer to part
1 of this question is that the authority for expenditure was minute of treasury board No. 438,477, dated November 14, 1952.
The answer to part 2 is Computing Devices of Canada Limited.
The answer to part 3 is yes. This project was cancelled in July, 1956, and in June, 1957, the former government issued a cabinet directive transferring the trainer to the Department of Transport. Arrangements were made by the Department of Transport with the civil aeronautic authority for the trainer to be converted to an air traffic control simulator by Computing Devices of Canada Limited, the cost of such conversion being met by the civil aeronautic authority. It is expected that this conversion will be completed in April, and the trainer will then be moved to the C.A.A. establishment in Indianapolis where it will be used by both D.O.T. and C.A.A. It has been agreed that C.A.A. will rent the equipment for the nominal sum of $1 per year.
The answer to part 4 is that the decision to cancel the project was taken on July 24, 1956. The expenditure on the project was $5,052,617.55. The answer to part 5 is that the building in which the trainer was to be housed comprises 75,655 square feet. The space allocated for the trainer was 35,000 square feet. The proportionate cost of the 35,000 square feet is $700,000.
The answer to part 6 is that this space is to be used for the accommodation of an alternative trainer, which has now been ordered

from the United Kingdom at a cost of $900,000. This is to be installed during 1958-59.

On Monday, January 13, the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary asked the following question:
I have a question for the Secretary of State for External Affairs of which I have given him notice.

Would he care to comment on Canada's position with respect to the neutrality drive of the Soviet government for the establishment of a buffer zone in Europe?
I presume, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member was referring to what has come to be known as the "Polish plan" for the setting up of an atomic-free zone in Europe. In his letter to the Prime Minister of December 13, Mr. Bulganin referred to this plan. I can best answer that question by reading a few sentences from the reply the Prime Minister tabled yesterday to the first Bulganin letter:
-we are studying the comments which * you made on a proposal put forward earlier by Poland for the creation of a zone in central Europe free of nuclear armaments. Mr. Speaker, last week the hon. member for Rosthern asked me a question regarding quotas on the delivery of grain in the prairie provinces. I promised to give him a reply on Monday, but I deferred it because of the general interest in other subjects.
This question is one which does not permit of a short answer, and is actually a type of question which simply asks for a repetition in the house of material already available in public documents. As the hon. member for Assiniboia pointed out the other day, the Canadian wheat board statistical summary gives the quota position in considerable detail.

But perhaps the hon. member for Rosthern was interested in just the general situation, and the answer is that taking the prairie provinces as a whole the main difference between the position now and a year ago is that the board has not yet authorized any 4-bushel general quotas. The number of delivery points on 2 and 3-bushel general quotas are about the same as a year ago.

Mr. Speaker, I wonder if I might ask a supplementary question. Would the minister say what action is being taken to equalize the quotas in the various provinces? As he will know, quotas in Manitoba are relatively low; Saskatchewan is in the middle, with Alberta relatively high. Can he say what action will be taken to attempt to equalize quotas by the end of the crop year.	__

The matter is, of course, under constant study, but the hon. member is fully aware of the conditions which have caused the disparity among the three provinces. The delivery quotas in Alberta and Saskatchewan compare favourably with the position a year ago as a result of heavy shipments of grain from those provinces to the Pacific coast, and from Saskatchewan out through Fort Churchill. In Manitoba the quotas have not advanced as rapidly as in the other two provinces, because shipments through Fort William and Port Arthur have not been of the same magnitude as a year ago.
I wonder what action is being taken or contemplated to increase shipments of grain eastward in order that Manitoba quotas may be increased?

I think the hon. member will recall that when we were announcing the recent wheat deal with India we indicated that half the quantity would be shipped through the Atlantic ports as a direct measure to ease the situation and enlarge the delivery quotas in Manitoba and eastern Saskatchewan.

Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that the minister could have given the number of points in each province on the respective quotas. It is true that this detailed information is available to hon. members, but it seems to me that there is a general interest in the comparative position with regard to the delivery points in each province; how many are on quotas of 1 bushel, 2 bushels, 3 bushels and 4 bushels, and whether any are on 5 bushels in any province. In view of the interest which I believe the house generally has in this matter I do not see why the minister does not give us this general picture.

Mr. Speaker, I should be very glad to furnish information of this nature and any other information of the kind which the hon. gentleman may require, but I do not think that would be in an oral answer, but rather that it would be a question for the order paper.

The reason I did not put it on the order paper was that when I put a similar question on the order paper it took six weeks for the government to answer.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct another question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I was not sure what the minister's position was in the matter. Do I take it that on this important question of grain delivery quotas he wishes that question put on the order paper; or will he answer it in the house today or when he is able to get the information as to the relative positions in regard to grain delivery quota points in Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba?

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is worried about my position on this matter. It is very clear and very sound. I suggest that his question should properly be placed on the order paper because the answer involves statistical information which should not be given orally.
Mr. Speaker, I submit that the information could be given-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. There seems to be a tendency today to carry forward at this stage an argument which may be relevant later on and which was perhaps relevant yesterday. The hon. member has had his answer, and I agree that that is the sort of question that would be better placed on the order paper.

Mr. Speaker, once again a case has been brought to my attention where the figures for registrations at the national employment service are being used as an official government figure for jobless in Canada. The house resumed, from Saturday, January 18, consideration of the motion of Mr. Harkness for the second reading of Bill No.

237, to provide for the stabilization of the prices of agricultural commodities, and the amendment thereto of Mr. McCullough.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is my first opportunity to make some remarks with regard to the bill respecting farm price stabilization. Hon. members will know that I am not at my best as an orator but am possibly a little more effective on the saxophone. Of course the rules of the house preclude the use of that offensive weapon, and also it would be against the regulations of the piccolo players' union. However, I am going to do my best to play a few tunes on this particular legislation without the instrument to which I am accustomed.
I think the first question that comes to our minds is why we should have this bill at all. It replaces the Agricultural Prices Support Act introduced by the former government in 1944, and is essentially very similar in its nature. The former legislation was an insurance policy against drastic drops in agricultural prices, and the legislation now before us fulfils the same function. They are both just that and nothing more.
I think the main reason why new legislation had to be introduced was not that it does any more than the former legislation, but that certain promises had been made and there had to be at least some attempt made that might look like fulfilment of those promises. We all know, of course, that the position of the farmer is not as good as it was a few years ago so far as his share of the national income is concerned, and that it is desirable to give him a larger share. That promise was made to our farmers by the government now in power during the last election campaign.
I know when I quote from the document I hold in my hand hon. members opposite will want to know what I am reading from. This book is entitled "3,001 Promises, By Saskatchewan's Most Promising Son, John G. Diefenbaker, Q.C.". It was compiled by the press of Canada and published by a very reputable Ottawa organization that is well known and appreciated from coast to coast, the national Liberal federation.
I am only going to quote very briefly. In his opening campaign speech in Toronto the new Prime Minister had this to say with regard to the desirability of doing something for the farmers of the country: "We will assure the farmer of his fair share of the national income." We also find that on April 26 the Globe and Mail reported him as saying that "farmers would get their fair share of the national income."

But I do not think they will under this bill. In fact the bill will not put one thin red dime into my constituency from the point of view of building up the income of the farmer above what it now is. However, these were the promises that were made at that time, and Bill No. 237 is supposed to be the fulfilment of those promises. I am happy that the bill has been introduced and that it has been so firmly established that it represents the answer to supplying the farmer with a fair share of the national wealth. On Monday the Prime Minister said that the Conservatives had already fulfilled that promise. I take it he was referring to this bill and the one having to do with cash advances on farm-stored grain.
I believe the Minister of Finance also said in his remarks yesterday that they had already fulfilled their promises to the farmers through the legislation before the house and that already passed. I am glad to have these statements on the record if this legislation is supposed to be the fulfilment of the promises made. I am reminded of a story I once heard about two hunters. Of course when hunters get together they are inclined to reminisce about their hunting prowess. One of them said he had been out in the province of Saskatchewan hunting ducks in the fall, and that with one shot from his shotgun he had brought down seven ducks. The second hunter agreed that was quite a feat, but he said, "You were using a shotgun with a lot of pellets in one shell. And in Saskatchewan the ducks are so thick that I do not think it is a particularly great feat to knock down seven with a shell of that kind."
The second hunter went on to say, "I was hunting in the province of Quebec with a .22 rifle using .22 short ammunition. I saw a fox standing in front of a large rock. I took dead aim at the fox and shot it, but the bullet bounced off the rock and knocked a squirrel out of a tree." The first hunter said, "That is not too bad for a single shot, but all you got was two animals and you must remember that I got seven with the shot I fired." The second hunter said, "I have not finished my story. I was standing on the bank of a stream at the time I fired my rifle and the recoil was so great that I fell over backward into the stream. When I got up my pants were so full of fish that a button flew off and killed a partridge."
It may be that there is a moral to that story for the government, the moral being that if you go hunting in Quebec you had better be careful about flying buttons.

speechtext: I hope the hon. member is going to relate this to the bill.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I am going to relate it to the bill. I intend to do so now because I think it is very relevant. You might say that story is a slight exaggeration of the truth, and definitely the bill before us is an exaggeration of what is going to be done for the farmers of western Canada particularly.
It has been suggested that the bill should be referred to the standing committee on agriculture, but in my opinion it could be more appropriately sent to another organization. In the United States there is an organization called the Burlington liars' club. Tall stories can be entered in contests they hold. If one were to take this bill and put a heading on it indicating what it is supposed to do, namely provide our farmers with a fair share of the national wealth, it would stand a pretty fair chance of winning first prize if it were entered in such a contest. This would bring some United States dollars into the treasury, and that might be very welcome as our trade with that country drops.
In so far as the bill itself is concerned, I do not like to be too rough on the minister because I do not think he had too much to do with the contents of this bill. I have a very high regard for the minister, but I think he was caught between two fires. In the first place, a promise had been made, a promise that should be fulfilled because there is nothing wrong with giving the farmers some share in the wealth of this country. If you honestly intend to do that it is very easily done. There have been occasions in the past when it has been deemed desirable that some segment of the population obtain a better share of the national wealth. I have in mind, as a precedent, the children of this country. It was found desirable that they be given a little better living standard. In order to do that we just sent them a monthly cheque and called it a family allowance. The same thing has been done in the way of pensions for the aged and so on. It is not difficult, therefore, if you actually want to give somebody a share in the wealth of the nation.
However, this measure is not going to do that job any more than the earlier measure did. The price support act passed in 1944 was never advertised as a measure to give the farmer his share of the national wealth. At that time, of course, the farmer was obtaining a fairly substantial share of the wealth of this country. This bill is nothing more than a duplicate of the other measure which was designed as insurance against any drastic drop in agricultural prices. As


an insurance policy it is a very desirable thing to have, and it does not make too much difference whether the insurance is obtained under this bill or the old bill. I have no particular criticism of this bill if they call it what it is, and that is an insurance policy against a drop in prices. If the government tries to tell farmers this measure will give them a share of the national wealth, then I must disagree entirely.
Why should we change from the act we have? What was wrong with the act we had? Why could not the act have been amended or changes made in it without introducing legislation into the house? I assume such a course would not have met the requirements of the Conservative party, because they had promised something and they wanted to make it appear as if they were fulfilling that promise.

speechtext: Are you going to vote against it?

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
My friend asks me if I am going to vote against it. I am going to answer that question directly. If you would, by any chance, look the other way when I am voting, Mr. Speaker, I would be pleased to vote for this bill twice because the sooner we get this measure into the hands of the farmers the sooner they can evaluate it. Right now they are getting a lot of eyewash about what this measure is going to do for them. The proof of the pudding is always in the eating, and believe me the eating is not going to be as good as the minister and the government have led the farmers to believe. In short, we have been told there are a lot of plums in this cake, but there are not going to be too many plums found in it when it comes to the actual eating.
So much for why we have to have a bill at all. A lot of window dressing is required to cover the promise that has been made. I do not blame the Minister of Agriculture for this at all because, as I say, he is caught between two fires. On the one hand he has a promise to fulfil, and on the other hand he has to obtain money from the treasury in order to fulfil it. I believe the Minister of Finance has said, "Doug, just go right ahead but do not cost us any money. If you want an extra $50 million in the pot and I only have to make an entry in the ledger, so the money is not going to leave the office, then that is fine with me."
Therefore we have this change from the old act, and instead of a $200 million revolving fund we have a revolving fund of $250 million. The minister has told us during this session that they are using only $30 million of the old $200 million fund

and $170 million is lying idle. He is going to add another $50 million to the idle fund to make it $220 million. This is not going to hurt the Minister of Finance, nor is it going to put any more money in the hands of the farmers.
I want to discuss this measure particularly in the light of what it does for the western farmers. I said I was going to play a few tunes on it, and if I had my saxophone perhaps I would start with "Home Sweet Home". However, I would find that song not quite appropriate to this bill because I come from the west, and this measure does not do anything for the west. The only fundamental change in this bill from the old price support measure, so far as the western farmers are concerned, is a change in the name. Instead of the old Agricultural Prices Support Act we will now have the agricultural prices stabilization act, the only change being the substitution of the word "stabilization" for the word "support". This is not going to put any money in the western farmers' pockets. Western grain is specifically excluded from this measure, and grain is their main source of income.

The hon. gentleman says "hear, hear". I wonder whether the people from the west will say "hear, hear" after they see this bill. On every previous occasion when we have had a Tory prime minister from the west, rather than doing things for the west, he did things to the west. This hon. gentleman is carrying on in the same tradition. In the first instance he turned down the British free trade offer. In the second place, and something that showed the sectional and regional views of the Tory party, we are no longer getting the dam the construction of which he promised would be started in December of last year. Instead, if we want to get in on the cheap power policy of this government we are obliged to move to New Brunswick or Nova Scotia.
Now we have this bill, and written right into it by this gentleman from the west, who is supposed to be doing things for western Canada and not to it, is the exclusion of all farmers in the west from any benefits as far as grain is concerned. But as long as they move to some other place they can come under the provisions of this bill.
There is nothing new about this Conservative procedure, Mr. Speaker. We have had these things in the past from Mr. Bennett. He did the same thing. I would suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that if we have any more of these Tory champions of the west coming here as prime minister, we shall soon have a desert out in the west, because people will be obliged to move to other parts of the country in order to enjoy the amenities which ordinary Canadians enjoy. If they want power they must go to the maritimes. If they want


the price support which everybody else enjoys, they must move to eastern Canada.

speechtext: What about natural gas?

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.

The hon. gentleman mentions natural gas. I am going to point this out to the hon. member for Peel, who is always helpful. I should make him my parliamentary assistant. That is another matter in which we are discriminated against in the west. You say you do not want any United States capital in there yet that is what has put Alberta on its feet. Then we have another policy of this government that will not allow natural gas, of which we have a great deal in both Alberta and Saskatchewan, to go out of the country to where there is a market.
I am glad the hon. gentleman points up these discriminatory Tory policies, because that is one thing I had forgotten. This is done under a Prime Minister who is supposed to be doing things for the west and who is now doing things to us. I had three items I wanted to mention, and that makes four. He has been in office for only about six or seven months. That is a very good record for somebody who is supposed to come from the west and who is already doing things to us.
As far as this bill is concerned-and I refer to the first section-it has a discriminatory section written into it, and in that regard it differs from the other bill. I want to discuss the differences between this bill and the previous one. This is the first thing; it is discriminatory against western farmers.
The next item is that we have $50 million more in the pot than we had before. That means exactly nothing, because it is only a bookkeeping entry in the treasury department. As I said, we are not now using $170 million of the $200 million that was available under the last act. I want to make this point. If you are going to do away with the other act of course you must have this one, and it does no more or no less than the other. But the government are putting flowers on it in order to try to sell it to the farmers. They are not going to sell it. I hold in my hand the death warrant of any Conservative candidate running in a farming area in western Canada. I hold in my hand Bill No. 237. I would also say that I hold my own passport to this place after the next election.

The third point that was written out in this bill is this. We have a board. The Prime Minister in the debate in the last couple of days said the price support bill did not have a board. I find that statement hard to line up with the minister saying that what we should have is flexibility in this bill. A board is going to make the bill less flexible. I should like to know what farmer out west is going to be happy because this bill has a board mentioned in it. I would say that a board, on the occasion the government requires it, is there to give the maximum of delay in action and does not provide anything else.

The other item provided is a committee. There was a committee of an advisory nature under the last bill and this one is a committee of farmers and heads of farm organizations. I see the hon. member for Brant-Haldimand looking at me. I should like to quote him on this very matter in this debate. He has outlined two functions of this committee fairly well. As reported at page 3480 of Hansard the hon. member said this:
This committee is to be composed of farmers and representatives of farm organizations. If those representatives are not satisfied with the way in which the government conducts itself,-
In other words, if they do not like the prices that the government support.
-having received the advice of that committee, there is only one thing they have to do and that is to resign from the committee. Until that time is reached they must accept, and I have no doubt they will accept, part of the responsibility for the prices that are set.
So here is a committee to take some responsibility, but as soon as it does not agree with the government it must resign. The parliamentary assistant to the minister has already told this committee where it can go, in no uncertain terms. It must take responsibility, but that is all. I will ask this question of the Minister of Agriculture; he does not need to answer it before I am through. Does this bill in the final analysis not come down to this; that apart from boards or advisory committees or anything else which might be put into the measure, action in the final analysis means a decision of the minister and of the government?
That is exactly what was provided in the last act. The government could do anything under the last act that it can do under this proposal; and there was no necessity, as I see it, for bringing in a new and flowery piece of legislation such as this present bill which the minister is trying to foist upon the farmers as something new.

The parliamentary assistant to the minister said you could judge the sincerity of the government by this bill. I think he is quite right in saying that, because this bill is the most insincere piece of legislation I have ever seen. He went on to say, further, that the farmer is in as serious a position today as he was in the thirties. And this is what he offers to farmers, presuming they are in that condition. I do not agree with him that the position today is as serious as it was in the thirties. It is bad, but not that bad. But if they were in such a position this is what he would offer them, to help the farmers out of their trouble.
I think that is in accord with previous Conservative policy. While we were in the depression of the thirties Mr. Bennett was in office, and he made a similar proposition. He said, "We will help the farmers out west, and any of them who have any wheat will be given five cents a bushel premium for what they grow". Unfortunately at that time, and Mr. Bennett knew it quite well, there were not five farmers in a hundred who had any wheat at all. The result was that to those who had, more was added, while those who had not were sent empty away. But I think that compares favourably with the position taken by the parliamentary assistant when he said this was the help necessary to the farmers, if they were in as bad a position as they were in the thirties.
The parliamentary assistant then said that this measure has another function, namely to guarantee prices. Just what prices does it guarantee? He said prices would be based on not less than 80 per cent of the average price over the 10-year period, a sliding base period. I agree that it is a sliding period. It is possible that the price could slide right into the basement; it could keep going down. In fact it could go down to zero and you could have a guaranteed price which was 80 per cent of nothing. If this is a guarantee the question is raised, what is a guarantee? I do not think this represents a guarantee.
Mr. Speaker, I have gone through five different points in this bill and the only one that means anything to western farmers, or which affects western farmers, is the name. The government has changed the word "support" to "stabilization".
Hon. members opposite will probably go out during an election campaign and say this is a great bill. I do not care what they say about it, because it is the farmers who will make the decision in the final analysis. So when somebody asks me whether I intend to vote for this bill, I say I will be glad to vote for it twice, having regard to the Prime

And I would suggest that if a farmer supports the government by supporting a Conservative candidate he is giving assent to the government's contention that they are providing him through this bill and the one which preceded it, the cash advance legislation, with a fair share of the national income. Every farmer in the west who agrees that that is being done for him by these two pieces of legislation deserves everything he will not get from this and the other measure. speechtext: Why are you voting for it, then?

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I have explained that. I do not explain it with any timidity, either. I am glad this bill has been brought in. I am glad to support it, so that it may be brought to the tribunal of the farmers themselves. They will certainly pass judgment on it, and they will not put their stamp of approval on it. In fact, Mr. Speaker, when it comes to a vote I am happy to support any kind of legislation upon which the government places its stamp of approval, merely to bring it before the public so that they can test the cake by eating it; and they will find that a lot of the cake they have been promised, and which they thought would contain so many raisins, is going to contain some very sour dough by the time they get it.
If this bill and the one preceding it are the answer to sharing the national wealth with the farmers, I am sure it is a long way off the mark. It was conceived in desperation during the election campaign, to secure votes; it was born in this house in hesitation, because it was changed three times-we have had three bills before us before we have got through second reading-it was received by the farmers with consternation and frustration, and it will finally be the annihilation of those who offer this insurance against disaster from too low farm prices.
I think the sooner this is put before the farmers the better for their own good, and I will be surprised if, on the basis of this legislation, I am not here to discuss the matter further after the next election.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think since the pipe-line debate raged in this house has a government presented a more unpopular measure than the bill now before us.


The agricultural producers of this country took this government seriously during the election campaign, believing it meant what it said when it promised a system of support prices which would be based on an adequate parity relationship. They believed the government meant what it said when it promised to provide prices for agricultural products which would give to agricultural producers their fair share of the national income. But the bill which is now before the house in amended form is an absolute and complete repudiation by the government of its own campaign pledge to provide adequate parity for agricultural producers.
I am amazed that the Prime Minister should have allowed such a bill to come before the house, though I am quite certain that the Minister of Agriculture thinks the bill is all right, because the record of the minister over the years is not one that would suggest he is in favour of adequate support prices. You can read the Hansard record since the Minister of Agriculture came into this house, and you will not find in that record one single speech in which the hon. gentleman stood up and asked for an adequate price support program that would give the agricultural producers of this country adequate parity.
Instead of that the record of the Minister of Agriculture in this house is one of opposition to motions that have been moved by hon. members in this group asking for adequate support prices. Not since he came to this house has the minister said he believed in stable marketing to the point where he thought the Canadian wheat board should be the sole agency buying and selling oats and barley. However, I had expected that the Prime Minister's attitude would be different, because over the years his record in this house is clear. He has fought for parity prices; the words are in the record. Sometimes he moved motions toward that end, and sometimes he voted for them.

An hon. member has said, "He got out most of the time." Perhaps the hon. member can say that, but I do not think I could make that statement. Nevertheless I am shocked that in the light of his record the Prime Minister should have given his stamp of approval either to the original bill or to this amendment of the original bill.
There is another thing I could not believe at first, although I think it is true now because I have heard it said so often. It is that the ordinary member of the Conservative party did not know what would be contained

in the original bill, nor was there a caucus held before that bill was introduced.

You can get up and deny it if you like, but I have been told that by members of the Conservative party. They told me that as backbenchers they were not consulted, though the backbenchers in that party represent agricultural producers in many ridings. The Minister of Agriculture did not take them into his confidence in a caucus and tell them what he intended to do, so no wonder when the original bill was brought in the backbenchers on the other side of the house representing agricultural constituencies were horrified that the government was bringing in this bill as its version of adequate parity.
The press is full of many comments on the hurried meetings that were held and the consultations of the Minister of Agriculture with the farm organizations and the pressure that was applied. The minister is a proud man, but he swallowed his pride when he brought in the amendments. He said the amendments did not mean there was any difference in the principle. I am quite sure he is right on that score. Since he is the man who is going to administer the bill he should know what the amendments mean. He explained that the reason he took the 10-year average was that the farm organizations told him that the prices during the past year had not been satisfactory and so he went back and included five of the best years. Then, as reported at page 2653 of Hansard of December 20, 1957, the minister went on to say:
I personally favour the three-year moving average formula-
He replaced the three-year moving average formula with the 10-year moving average formula because the farm organizations said the three-year formula was no good. The 10-year formula is not much better, but it is a slight improvement. The Minister of Agriculture said he was changing the formula, but that he was not convinced and still thought the three-year moving average was the best.
This legislation has been before the house off and on for some months, and I have yet to hear of a single farm organization which has placed its stamp of approval on it. I have yet to see a letter from an individual producer who thinks the government has fulfilled its pledge. I am quite prepared to admit that the government might accomplish something under this legislation. It might, in fact, improve agricultural prices under this bill, just as it was theoretically possible for the previous government to improve prices under 96698-229i
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization its legislation. But if the government does improve agricultural prices under the bill that is before us there will be a suspicion abroad in this country that the prices have been improved just for the forthcoming election campaign, for a period of one year, or just long enough to get the government by; because there is no guarantee under this legislation that prices will be maintained on an adequate parity basis.
Following this the minister, in order to substantiate his case, said "Look at all the trouble the Americans are in." Well, it is true that the Americans are in some trouble, but as a wheat producer I would love to get into that same kind of trouble. When I haul a bushel of good wheat I receive $1.20. If the wheat is an inferior grade I receive much less. The United States producer, on the other hand, receives $2 a bushel for his wheat. Does he receive a cash advance for half of a 6-bushel quota at a rate of 50 cents a bushel? Not at all. He receives a cash advance of $2 a bushel on 90 per cent of all the wheat he has threshed. The minister rose in this house and said Mr. Benson says they are in trouble in the United States.

The farmers in the United States are in trouble precisely because the secretary of agriculture in that country has followed the same kind of policy of which our Minister of Agriculture now approves. With the possible exception of Mr. Dulles I do not think there is a man in a responsible position in the United States at this time who is more discredited than the United States secretary of agriculture. The event that happened in the recent United States election is precisely what happened in Canada in the recent Canadian election.
We who represent agricultural constituencies in the main are very often told that we represent a dwindling portion of the nation's population and that we are not very important. If anyone will look at the election records of this country and the United States he will see that the farmers in both countries exercise an extremely important influence on the results of elections. The farmers more than any other single group in this country are responsible for defeating the Liberal party on June 10. The farmers of the United States said to President Eisenhower and to the congress of the United States in the last election there that they did not like the Republican agricultural program, as a result the Republicans no longer control the congress of that country.
When the Minister of Agriculture in this country brings forth Mr. Benson's program

Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization and parrots Mr. Benson's statements to substantiate his own position, I say he is undermining the influence of the Conservative party in this country, because the people know that Mr. Benson, in the words of the senator who is chairman of the United States senate agriculture sub-committee, is proposing steps at this time to drive thousands of United States farmers off the land, and is threatening to destroy the very basis of United States agriculture. That is precisely what this government will do under this legislation if one is to judge from the statements made by the Minister of Agriculture up to the present time.
Oh, it is probably true that if hon. members of this house bring enough pressure to bear on the government it will do something for the farmer under this legislation, but all it will do is provide political prices for agricultural products; and the farmer is sick to death of political prices, because they certainly do not help the people they claim to be directed toward assisting. The position of the government is inadequate.
What is the position of the official opposition? It is weird and strange. Initially the former minister of agriculture damned this bill. Why, he said, it is practically the same as the one he had, which resulted in his being chased from office and in the Liberal party having the smallest representation from the three prairie provinces.

speechtext:
The old Agricultural Prices Support Act was the death warrant of the Liberal party and this agricultural prices stabilization legislation-and I agree with the hon. gentleman-will be the death warrant of the Conservative party. I am happy that both those old parties will now be destined to the grave. I think it is the best thing that could happen so far as the agricultural producers of this country are concerned.
In this session we have seen that there is no difference between those two parties. One is in and the other wants to be in. The Liberal party had been in so long that it does not know how to get back in now. It has been making the strangest speeches in this house, and the party passed the weirdest resolutions at their recent convention. Are they for something more for the farmer? Of course they are not. They have been out of office seven months, but they have learned nothing. They have been passing and approving the same old kind of discredited policy that they have promoted in this house. They have a four-page agricultural resolution with 16 subparagraphs, which was passed by the resolutions committee. It might have come out of the grass, but it was the brass that doctored it up and presented it to the convention, or perhaps it did not present it. As long as the resolutions committee passed it I suppose it is policy, that is Liberal democracy.

speechtext: You should not talk about democracy.

What did they say about parity prices? Nothing. What did they say about the great demand today to give deficiency payments to the agricultural producers of western Canada, and give them an adequate income? What did they say about the unanimous resolutions which have been passed by prairie farm organizations for deficiency payments? Well, their fourth resolution reads in this way:
Maintain and extend a system of support prices and deficiency payments-
It sounds good, but I continue:
-where appropriate-

I think that demolishes it. The resolution goes on:
-administered in such a way as to obtain for farmers for their products prices bearing a fair relationship to their costs of production and designed to ensure to farmers a fair share of the national income and encourage the production of marketable farm products.
It will be noted that they said "deficiency payments, where appropriate."
Their sixth resolution deals in some detail with their wheat policy, but they did not mention a word about the great drive for deficiency payments that is now being made, because obviously they are not in favour of deficiency payments. Well, that is a rather strong statement to make. I have been listening to members of the official opposition discuss this question. They have not asked for any deficiency payments on wheat; they have not asked for the 20-cent deficiency payment that is now the fulcrum of the great drive on the prairies for justice for the agricultural producers.
They have not mentioned it, but I have evidence to show what they think of it, and from a very good friend of the members of the opposition. I hold in my hand an article in the Regina Leader-Post dated January 13, 1958. It was written by E. N. Davis, who is an associate editor of the Leader-Post. I do not think there is any stronger supporter of the Liberal party anywhere in Canada than the Regina Leader-Post. This man was travelling on the train with the Saskatchewan delegation and he had a chance to be with them in their intimate conversation. He was in the back room to use a phrase with these men on the train, and this is what he says:
Strong opposition against the deficiency payment system advocated by the Saskatchewan wheat pool and the Canadian Federation of Agriculture was evident. The inclination was to scoff at the practicability and desirability of hand-outs of many millions of dollars to the farmers from the federal treasury.
Such hand-outs, it was contended would encourage grain production and the accumulation of still larger surpluses, and discourage the movement from the land of farmers who lack the land and capital to farm economically.
The people on the prairies today are united as never before in their demand for deficiency payments, and the Liberal party in opposition is strongly opposed to the people on the prairies. We have heard about the death warrant of the Conservative party. This statement constitutes the death warrant of the Liberal party in western Canada in the next election.

Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at one o'clock I had been saying that although the people on the prairies are united as they have never been before in asking the government for deficiency payments, apparently the Liberal convention overlooked supporting deficiency payments on grain. In fact it is reliably reported that the Saskatchewan delegates to the convention were opposed to such payments.
I had said that the tactics of the official opposition were very difficult to understand. After the hon. member for Meadow Lake had said that the bill now before us was so bad that it would mean the death of the Conservative government, I was absolutely amazed that he should say that he proposes to vote for this legislation when he considers it so bad and the government so ill advised as to have introduced it.
In asking for deficiency payments the people on the prairies are doing so because they are caught in a terrible cost-price squeeze. Since the end of the war the cost of production has gone up more than 50 per cent and the prices of agricultural products have fallen by more than 7 per cent. In asking for deficiency payments they realize the very low prices that are being paid for the grain that is sold. They realize that apparently the day is rapidly approaching when interim and final payments on oats and barley will become a thing of the past, and that so far as wheat is concerned there will probably only be one payment in the future, with the price for the current crop year being lower than it has been in recent years.
The price of oats is so low today that oats are being sold at exactly the initial price of 66 cents a bushel, so the oat pool will suffer a very substantial net loss involving a cost to the treasury. No. 1 feed barley is selling for 87J cents a bushel, which is half a cent a bushel above the initial price for the main grade of barley, so the producers cannot look forward to an interim or final payment on the barley crop.
The reasons for which they are asking for deficiency payments on the 1955-56 crop are becoming greater and stronger as the days go by. What are they asking? They are asking for a payment of 20 cents a bushel out of the national treasury on the 1955-56 crop. They are asking for comparable payments for barley and oats for the same period. Agricultural experts have always said that the price of barley should be about two-thirds the price of wheat, and that the price of oats should be about half the price of wheat. Using the same proportions for deficiency payments,

Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization I suggest that the wheat pools and the prairie people will be asking for at least as much and perhaps more on the 1956-57 accounts whenever they are closed.
The prairie people are deadly earnest in asking that the federal government today pay deficiency payments on wheat, oats and barley for the 1955-56 crop, amounting to approximately $95 million; and undoubtedly they will be asking for at least as much for the next pool period. They are asking for a payment of $190 million from the national., treasury.
Oh, I know there will be outcries in certain quarters if the government decides to use deficiency payments in those crop years to bolster the falling incomes of the prairie grain producers, but I suggest that such payments are valuable and necessary not only to the people to whom they will be made but also to the Canadian economy at the present time. Yesterday the Minister of Finance suggested in one part of his speech that the government was prepared to budget for a deficit if that was necessary to solve the unemployment problem.
That was good news. I suggest that as a first step	in	budgeting	for a deficit	thegovernment should announce deficiency payments on	the	grain in	question and	paysubstantial sums of money to the prairie producers.	If	that were	done it would	notonly help	the	incomes	of people on	the
prairies, but the money going into circulation through being spent on goods produced in Canada would have a very beneficial effect as far as unemployment is concerned.
When I was in Saskatchewan during the Christmas recess I discussed this bill and the matter of deficiency payments with people representing all the farm organizations, people who in the past have supported every political party represented in the House of Commons. Their unanimous opinion was that unless the federal government agreed to a deficiency payment on the 1955-56 crop year a mass delegation of prairie people to Ottawa should be organized. They did not have in mind just a delegation of farmers. They spelled out the people they felt should be included in the delegation. They said it should contain representatives of businessmen, representatives of the urban municipalities, the teachers' federation, the rural municipal secretaries, the clergy and homemakers' associations, a cross section of the people of western Canada.
There is a precedent for such a large delegation, because in 1942, some 400 from Saskatchewan came to Ottawa to wait upon the government and ask for a substantial increase in the price of wheat. At a later

date, as a result of that delegation appearing in Ottawa a very substantial increase was made in the price of wheat. I say to the government at this time, therefore, that if they insist upon promoting a bill which guarantees no more to the producers than is guaranteed by this bill, that is merely an encouragement to the people of the prairies to organize this mass delegation to come to Ottawa, of which they are talking so much at the present time.
The minister says he does not want a parity formula in the bill. He has refused to put any kind of parity formula in the bill, even though the Canadian Federation of Agriculture have said that their main request is for a 70 per cent parity formula. I want to say immediately that I do not believe 70 per cent is enough, but the point I am making is that even though the Canadian Federation of Agriculture asks for 30 per cent less than full parity, which in almost every if not every instance is lower than the market prices of these commodities today, the government has refused. The government has not only refused to put in a formula, but they have refused to put in a formula that at the moment would cost the treasury little or nothing.
I do not understand the attitude of the government. I do not understand the attitude of the minister. I do not know why he should oppose putting this formula in the bill, unless he is prepared to let prices go lower and lower until they are very much below even the 70 per cent parity formula. I am making a special plea now to the government and to the members on the government side of the house to accept-

I wonder what the government really has in mind for the producers when they will not accept this very modest request. I question the sincerity of the government in doing something adequate under this bill over a long period of time. I am not saying they will not do something soon. I am not saying they will not do something in the face of an election. I question their sincerity to do the right thing over a long period of time.

Why do I question their sincerity? Because they have had the Agricultural Prices Support Act available to them since June 21, when they took office, and although agricultural commodity prices have been low during that period they have not used the powers available to increase agricultural prices. Apparently they never really intended to improve the prices of agricultural products or the incomes of producers by reasonable amounts. I know of no sensible reason why the government did not use the instrument available, the Agricultural Prices Support Act, to improve the prices of agricultural commodities.
How often have I heard Conservative members condemn the previous administration for the low floor price on eggs? Has anything been done to increase that floor price? No. We get the same kind of glib assurances from this Minister of Agriculture as we got from the last one, that steps are being taken to hold up the floor price. All the time the producers know they are being chiselled and rooked by the packers of this country. There is no guarantee that grades are carried through to the consumer. The government has done no more in the last seven months than the previous administration did to increase prices of farm products. The price of hogs has fallen by 12 cents a pound, from 35 cents to 23 cents, but nothing was done to increase the support price for hogs.

The longer the debate goes on the worse the situation becomes. The hon. member now says we have not the facilities. We have not a decent bill. We have not really got support prices, and now we have not any facilities. We have not a government that wants to do something, and that is quite clear. We have a government that has presented a bill which is political window dressing to blind a number of people who put faith in them and thought they really meant to do something.
The federation of agriculture has calculated what the proposed support prices for the various agricultural commodities would be on the 80 per cent basis. I have taken these prices and reduced them by the amount of inflation since 1935, to get comparable figures in terms of real purchasing power in 1935. I find that although hogs sold for 12 cents a pound in 1935, in the middle of the depression, the guaranteed price under this 80 per cent clause of 23.36 cents a pound would be only 8.6 cents in terms of 1935 dollars, a worse position for the producer than 1935. The price of beef was 6 cents a pound in 1935, and under this plan it would be 6.45 cents in terms of real purchasing power. The wholesale price of eggs was 31 cents in 1935, and would be 16.8 cents in terms of the same dollars under this bill. The wholesale price of butter in 1935 was 23 cents a pound, and under this legislation would be 18 cents a pound in terms of real purchasing power.
The basic and absolute guarantee under this bill, therefore, would be at a lower level and would place the producers of this country in a worse position than when they kicked out the last Conservative government that was

The brass had better start listening to the rumblings of the grass, because the 600,000 farm families are not prepared to be kicked out of their occupation without doing something about it.
The government have a lot of fine phrases in this legislation about the cost of production. The minister says that is the most important thing that is going to be considered, the cost of production. The figures for Alberta, based on studies made by the Alberta government, show that in 1955 in order to give efficient butter producers 58 cents an hour for their labour, the price of butter would have to be 85 cents a pound. The government's basic floor price in this legislation is 45 cents a pound. In order to give the farmer engaged in egg production 58 cents an hour for his labour, eggs would have to be 40 cents a dozen. Then the minister is saying, "Well, now, if you just leave it to me, I am going to get the price up from 28 cents or 29 cents a dozen to 30 cents a dozen".

I challenge the Minister of Agriculture to appear with me on any public platform in western Canada or in any other part of Canada, at a meeting sponsored by a bona fide farm organization, to discuss how under this legislation that is now being proposed he intends to condemn the agricultural producers of this country to an unfair share of the national income and how he intends to continue to regard people who produce in the agricultural industry as second class citizens.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker, for your help. Quite frankly I enjoy it this way myself, because I know who suffers as a result of these clashes.
The story I have been outlining concerning the pools is the story of how western Canada tried in its own way to meet this problem, but we had to face up to the fact that we needed federal help. In eastern Canada, of course, the farmers have gone in for producer boards as a means of stabilizing their prices.
I think an illustration of what I am talking about will paint the picture much clearer than anything else I could say. In Ontario and Saskatchewan one of our side products is turkeys. Consider a farmer who has had difficulty trying to sell his grain. He observes that the price of turkeys has gone up to anywhere between 45 and 50 cents a pound. He then decides that next year he is going to raise turkeys. He proceeds to purchase some turkeys and raise them; then when he is ready to market them in the fall he discovers that a large number of farmers in his area have had the same idea. When they go to sell their turkeys the price declines to 20 cents a pound, and all the farmers have lost their shirts. As a result it is difficult to persuade farmers to go into cash crops because of the uncertainty.
That is the reason for the stabilization bill. It is the first step in an effort to see if it is possible to get a group of farm representatives to sit down and look over the facts before us such as the cost of production, supply and demand and other relevant considerations, and then determine a price that will gauge the market in order to give a price that is close to the cost of production but which will not cause huge surpluses.
It must be very clear that if you produce too much then the support price the next year must be reduced as a warning to decrease production. If the support price does not produce enough, as in the case of butter, then we shall have to bring it up carefully until it does. Meanwhile the farmer who does produce each year knows that the support price will be announced before he puts in his crop, or before he breeds his animals. He will not lose his shirt, as in the case I have just given.
It is absolutely, clear, Mr. Speaker, that support prices must be flexible, or we will destroy the scheme with surpluses and the
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization farmer will be back to where he was before. In setting a support price the bill says:
The governor in council shall have regard to the estimated average cost of production of the commodity.
This is an effort on our part to set supports as close as possible to the cost of production without creating unmanageable surpluses. I believe it is a sensible approach and makes the plan workable.
I would like to say a word to those who have been peddling the propaganda in favour of a 100 per cent parity price system. The 100 per cent of parity is a magic figure. It seems to suggest to every farmer that he is going to get the full cost of production and a return on his investment; but it does not stand sober analysis, Mr. Speaker.
Any person with reasonable intelligence who thinks for a moment realizes that a 100 per cent parity price is a fallacy. Cost of production, according to most statistical and formal approaches, is based on the average cost; and the bitter truth is that this arbitrary average means the ruin of the small farmer, for a very simple reason. The reason is that the small farmer usually has costs of production above the average, and the large farmer has costs of production below the average.
In plain terms, an arbitrary 100 per cent parity price would be mainly an extra bonus to the big farmer.
In western Canada today nearly two-thirds of our farmers farm 300 acres or less; if the specified acreage is used as the measuring stick. These farmers need help; they need crop insurance, they need a farm credit program; they need to cut costs; they need producer boards to help them bargain, and they need some help in setting up those conservation methods which will help them to greater efficiency and lower costs. All these are part of our 13-point program.
I think the people of western Canada and of all Canada want to see any government put that policy into effect to see if it will help in lifting the farmers out of this lower standard of living into which they have fallen over the last few years, when the farmers who composed one-sixth of the population got only one-twelfth of the income of this country. I put before the house in all seriousness that this stabilized price legislation is the first step in any program to achieve this long-range program. If we are going to get farmers to shift from one product to another product where there is a higher return, we have to guarantee that if they make some investment they will have a price that will save them from losing out in that particular year. If we want to encourage

part-a section-of the act and not a recital or part of the preamble. I shall read from this section of the act:
In prescribing prices under paragraphs (a) and (c) of subsection (1), the board shall endeavour to ensure adequate and stable returns for agriculture by promoting orderly adjustment from war to peace conditions and shall endeavour to secure a fair relationship between the returns from agriculture and those from other occupations.
In other words, it prescribes the duty of this board to give the farmer a fair share of the national income. This is part of an act of parliament. Now we are asked to repeal this measure. I ask all members who represent farm constituencies to note that this bill now before us repeals this section which is part of the law of the land today, and proposes to replace it with a wishy-washy preamble. Anyone who knows anything about the interpretation of law knows that a preamble has not the same binding effect as something contained in the body of the act itself. The preamble in this bill is not even as definite as the section to which I have referred because it says:
Whereas it is expedient to enact a measure for the purpose of stabilizing the prices of agricultural commodities in order to assist the industry of agriculture to realize fair returns from its labour and investment, and to maintain a fair relationship between prices received by farmers and the costs of the goods and services that they buy;
This preamble, of course, has not the same force as the directive we find in the body of the Agricultural Prices Support Act, which is already the law of the land. What was written in here as an objective of this board was that they should endeavour to see that the farmer got a fair share of the national income, and now this government proceeds to introduce a measure which will replace that with something that is not even in the act itself but only in the preamble and which does not go nearly so far. He read paragraph 4 of the recently adopted Liberal platform in regard to agriculture. I should like to read it again, Mr. Speaker. Then I should like to make a short comment on it. It reads:
4. Maintain and extend a system of support prices and deficiency payments, where appropriate, administered in such a way as to obtain for farmers for their products prices bearing a fair relationship to their costs of production and designed to ensure to farmers a fair share of the national income and encourage the production of marketable farm products.
I was one of the committee which drafted this resolution. My hon. friend made some suggestion that this was drafted by the so called brass. I was a member of the committee and sat right through from start to finish in the drafting of this resolution. I want to say to you, Mr. Speaker, that if every party drafted up its resolutions with as careful consideration for the wishes of the people sent there by their constituencies to represent their wishes from all parts of Canada, they could say that they were having democratic processes operating fully. This resolution is the result of the combined representations from the whole country. It represents the wishes of Liberals from one end of Canada to the other. It was not drawn up by any brass. It was drawn up by the representatives of Liberals from all over Canada and is based upon their wishes. I think those who have known me for any length of time- I have been quite a while around here-know that when I say that I am telling nothing more than the straight truth. Any idea that this policy was dictated by anybody is completely incorrect.
The next thing I wish to mention is this. My friend the hon. member for Assiniboia made some slighting reference to the fact that in this program we said that we would advocate making deficiency payments where appropriate. The attitude of the farmers' organizations, all of them, including the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, was this: They took exactly that same attitude. They took the attitude that the primary way of supporting farm income is by maintaining prices for the product as high as possible but
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization where it is not possible, owing to the fact that we are a trading nation, to raise prices high enough to give the farmer a fair share of the national income, then bolster up his income by making deficiency payments. Everybody in this house knows very well that there is a strict limit on what you can do in raising farm income by raising support prices because, as has been pointed out by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture more than once, if you get prices of farm products much higher than prices, we will say, in the United States, then goods will flow in from the United States to get the benefit of those Canadian prices. That means that you are obliged to put on tariffs or embargoes against imports into Canada. Once you get embarked on a policy like that you are going to have reprisals taken against you and Canada is the last nation on earth which can afford to start any trade war or any system whereby embargoes and tariffs will be imposed against our exports of agricultural products.
As I pointed out in a previous speech on the resolution preceding this bill, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture took the attitude that you could only raise support prices to about 70 per cent of parity and that you could not raise them much higher than the price of similar products in the United States for the reason I have stated. Some years ago-two years ago, I believe-the Canadian Federation of Agriculture realized that this system of support prices, hedged in as it was by the inability to raise prices much higher than outside prices, was not enabling the Agricultural Prices Support Act to give the farmer a fair share of the national income.
They set up a committee to study this, and last July they changed their policy, and said: we should get the farmers as large a share of the national income as possible by maintaining support prices as high as possible. If that does not give the farmer a fair share of the national income you should then resort to deficiency payments. And they stated to the government in a memorandum last July that they had changed their policy with regard to asking for greater use of deficiency payments. I call the attention of the house to the fact that this statement was made to the government last July and that the election was in June. So the Canadian Federation of Agriculture had before that time only been asking for deficiency payments in cases largely limited to perishable products. But in July they came out for a system of raising the farmers income to a fair share of the national income by a more extended use of deficiency payments.
That, in my opinion, was a historic decision on the part of the Canadian Federation

What do we find? The government have introduced this bill to repeal the Agricultural Prices Support Act. They say that the main consideration under this bill will be the cost of production to the farmers. This was stated by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness). The Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources however speaking today referred in a most scathing way to the proposal of giving the farmer his cost of production. He stated, in effect, that giving a farmer his cost of production was a ridiculous attitude. But this is what the Minister of Agriculture said was the main purpose of the bill. In his speech, as reported on page 2652 of Hansard, he made this statement very clearly. He said:

If this is the purpose of the government, what becomes of the pretence that this bill is better than the Agricultural Prices Support Act, and what becomes of the attitude of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture that prices should be supported as high as possible and then the farmers income raised enough by deficiency payments to enable him to have a fair share of the national income?
The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) also had something to say about our failure at our convention to endorse deficiency payments with regard to wheat. I would point out to him that clause 4 of our agricultural program applies to all agricultural products-wheat, oats, barley and every other farm product. At the convention I drew to the attention of the committee dealing with this plank in the program what had been said to the cabinet on January 13 last in a submission by the wheat pools of the west. I want to read a few words from that submission made to the cabinet-the present cabinet-by the wheat pools on January 13 of this year. Here is what they said:
We believe, Mr. Prime Minister, that when you gave assurances that policies would be formulated


that would ensure an adequate parity for agricultural producers based on the cost-price relationship you had not overlooked the grain producers of western Canada, nor do we believe you have overlooked them now.
That is a charitable statement because nothing has been done by this cabinet so far to show that they have not overlooked this question. And so they asked, as they say, for an audience with the Prime Minister and they pointed out-I ask hon. members to note these figures-that since 1947 there has been an increase of 50.3 per cent in the cost of commodities and services used by western farmers, an increase of 50 per cent in costs in the course of practically 10 years. During the same period there had been a drop of 20.8 per cent in the average price of wheat on the farms. And, incidentally, I ask what has the present government done about that? It has done nothing, despite the fact that it has now been in office for seven months. The submission goes on to say:
We do not need to remind you, sir, or your colleagues, that wheat constitutes the main source of farm revenue in western Canada.
That being the case, how have they, the government kept their promise to raise the revenues of the farmers of western Canada? The submission goes on to point out that wheat deliveries have been up to the average deliveries during the previous years, and therefore that low farm income is not due to failure to make deliveries. It goes on to say:
During the period since 1947 in which the relationship of farm costs and farm prices has been showing an ever-widening divergence, other groups have taken steps to meet the problem of increasing costs.
I would ask hon. members representing other parts of Canada and other occupational groups to note these figures:
The gross national product which may be regarded as a barometer of economic activity has more than doubled.
I ask all hon. members to bear this in mind. The fall in the price that farmers received for their wheat has amounted to 20.8 per cent since 1947, whale the value of the gross national product of the people as a whole in Canada has more than doubled. The average weekly earnings of those employed in industry, exclusive of primary production industries, have increased to the extent of 77.3 per cent in that period. I ask hon. members to bear in mind that while farmers have had to suffer a reduction of what they realize on their wheat amounting to 20 per cent, wages have increased by 77 per cent. And then the submission goes on to say:
Including the 3.6 per cent increase in freight rates which has not yet been implemented, general freight rates have increased 120 per cent.

Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization
And then:
The general wholesale price index has risen 39.5 per cent.
After which, they say this:
In the face of these conditions all indicating there have been major adjustments in most segments of the economy, farmers are still required to sell their grain both for domestic consumption and for export at prices dictated by international price levels without regard to the spiralling costs of production, and without regard to the general high level of the Canadian economy.
The submission goes on to point out that Canada is one of the few countries whose farmers have to compete unassisted in world wheat markets against wheat offerings from countries which are heavily subsidized, and urge that the government take immediate steps to ensure that farm producers will receive a return for the production of their farms which would bear a fair relationship to cost of production and Canadian living standards. Further, they say:
If price supports and other policies fail to provide fair relationship prices on agricultural products, that deficiency payments be provided by the treasury of Canada.
This is exactly along the lines of the Liberal program. It proposed that where the price received by a farmer does not bring him a fair income, then deficiency payments should be made. This was why the words "where appropriate" were used. Does the hon. member for Assiniboia say we should have said we would give deficiency payments whether appropriate or not?
The Liberal party in drawing up this program tried to be very careful and reasonable in making to the people of Canada only what it felt were fair and reasonable promises which could be carried out. So when it is suggested that nothing was included in this program in regard to deficiency payments on wheat my answer is that I was present when this was discussed. If anyone will read the resolutions he will find that paragraph 6 said that we would maintain a Canadian wheat board and during periods of crop surplus the Liberal government would do certain things. But otherwise the general policy in regard to agriculture including deficiency payments was to be applied to the products of the western farmer the same as the eastern farmer. We felt that the western farmer was entitled as much as anybody else to deficiency payments in order to bring his income up to a fair level compared to that of other people. The idea was that the wheat board should handle the marketing of the farmer's grain but all the wheat board has to distribute is that for which it sells the grain and if a farmer is going to get any more it must be provided by the rest of the economy in the
form of deficiency payments to bring his income up to a fair level compared to that received by everybody else.
The thing I do not like about the present bill is that-
